answer.answer:
Leflunomide at rheumatoid-arthritis-relevant exposure restores myeloid differentiation in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia through on-target dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition

The hypothesis is that leflunomide restores myeloid differentiation and lowers leukemia-initiating activity in differentiation-arrested acute myeloid leukemia when free concentrations inhibit dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH). The exposure anchor is the drug's original indication, rheumatoid arthritis. Approval status, labeled indication, conversion to teriflunomide, protein binding, and clinically achieved free concentrations are unverified prior knowledge and require confirmation before dose selection. The biological context is AML in which a myeloid differentiation block is the dominant measurable lesion. The primary endpoint is a differentiation program—morphology, mature myeloid markers, and a transcriptional differentiation score—plus reduced leukemia-initiating activity. Bulk apoptosis, depletion of reactive-oxygen-species (ROS)-low stem cells, and persistence of cytarabine-residual cells are separate comparator endpoints.

Supported premises are limited to the packet. [S4] reports that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in those models, connecting a metabolic enzyme to release of differentiation blockade. [S4] leaves open whether an approved drug that affects this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity; that open question is the repurposing claim. [S1] reports that functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low ROS and elevated BCL-2, and that BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S2] reports that cytarabine-residual cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells and instead showed oxidative-metabolism and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. [S3] reports that venetoclax with azacitidine was linked to altered leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects. [S3] is an established regimen used here only as a mechanistic comparator. Efficacy in [S3] is not evidence about leflunomide.

Speculative bridges are explicit. The proposal assumes that teriflunomide inhibits human DHODH and that free levels attained in rheumatoid arthritis can overlap concentrations that drove differentiation in the systems summarized by [S4]. It assumes samples can be preselected for a DHODH-responsive differentiation block using a tool inhibitor. It assumes pyrimidine depletion is causal, so uridine repletion will reverse nucleotide loss and the differentiation phenotype together. It assumes a window versus normal hematopoietic progenitors at that exposure. These pharmacokinetic, on-target, subset, and selectivity assumptions are absent from [S1]–[S4].

Alternative explanations fit the same evidence. Differentiation-marker changes could reflect off-target activity. They could be secondary to oxidative-phosphorylation stress of the sort tied to BCL-2 inhibition in [S1] and to venetoclax–azacitidine in [S3]. Nucleotide stress could kill blasts while surface-marker shifts are bystanders. The cytarabine-residual oxidative state in [S2] could change sensitivity independently of DHODH. Matched injury to normal progenitors would eliminate a therapeutic window even if blast markers move.

The discriminating test uses primary AML cells and one genetically defined in vivo model, limited to samples with a differentiation block and a response to a tool DHODH inhibitor, following the experimental logic of [S4]. Leflunomide and teriflunomide are dosed across a range taken from independently verified pharmacokinetic sources. Comparators are vehicle, the tool DHODH inhibitor, venetoclax (BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation comparator from [S1] and [S3]), and cytarabine (residual-disease comparator from [S2]). Uridine co-treatment tests rescue. A DHODH-resistant allele or DHODH depletion, where feasible, tests genetic dependence. Prespecified readouts stay separate: differentiation (morphology, CD11b and CD14 or species-appropriate markers, colony maturation, transcriptional score); bulk viability and apoptosis; ROS-low functionally defined stem-cell frequency and oxidative-phosphorylation rate; burden after cytarabine; and matched normal CD34-positive progenitors with in vivo blood counts. A positive result requires increased differentiation and lower leukemia-initiating activity at a DHODH-inhibitory exposure that is less toxic to normal progenitors than to AML cells.

Falsifying observations are fixed in advance. The hypothesis fails if DHODH-inhibitory concentrations, documented by uridine-reversible pyrimidine depletion, leave myeloid differentiation indistinguishable from vehicle in the preselected models. It fails if anti-leukemic activity persists after uridine rescue or in a DHODH-independent genetic control. It fails if normal hematopoietic progenitors are depleted to the same degree as AML cells. It fails if leukemia reduction tracks oxidative-phosphorylation collapse in the venetoclax-sensitive ROS-low population in the absence of a differentiation program.

Limitations are built into the sources. [S4] does not name leflunomide, measure human exposure, or demonstrate selectivity. [S1] withholds any claim that a metabolic inhibitor has an acceptable window. [S2] keeps residual oxidative AML distinct from the ROS-low stem-cell population. [S3] cannot be reassigned to another drug. Genotype, subtype, and microenvironment may bound the response. Clinical efficacy is outside this proposal. Regulatory and pharmacokinetic statements remain unverified prior knowledge.

Pyrimidine depletion could kill cycling bulk blasts and leave both residual oxidative cells and ROS-low stem cells in place. Biological context. The proposed setting is primary or patient-derived AML blasts that retain a myeloid differentiation block and measurable de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The primary endpoint is acquisition of myeloid maturation, scored separately from bulk cytotoxicity, from depletion of ROS-low quiescent leukemia stem cells, and from clearance of cytarabine-residual oxidative cells. Matched normal CD34-positive hematopoietic progenitors are the selectivity comparator. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is treated only as an established metabolic comparator and is not the repurposing candidate [S3].

Supported premises. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the models investigated, linking pyrimidine metabolism to relief of differentiation blockade and supplying an alternative to nonspecific cell killing [S4]. Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the specimens studied often had low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2, and BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1]. Residual cells after cytarabine were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed oxidative-metabolism features, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related properties, and altering that state changed treatment response in those settings [S2]. Venetoclax with azacitidine has been connected to leukemia-stem-cell energy-metabolism changes, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, in patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up [S3]. These premises define comparators and endpoints. They do not show that an approved drug which affects DHODH reproduces the differentiation result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity [S4].

Unverified prior knowledge requiring checking. Teriflunomide is recalled as an approved oral medicine for relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis and as an inhibitor of dihydroorotate dehydrogenase. Leflunomide, recalled as approved for rheumatoid arthritis, is recalled as a prodrug that generates teriflunomide. Approval status, labeled indication, human unbound exposure, protein binding, marrow penetration, and the concentration–effect relationship for DHODH inhibition lie outside this packet and must be verified. No pharmacokinetic values are asserted.

Speculative bridges. First, if teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in differentiation-blocked AML blasts at unbound concentrations achieved during multiple-sclerosis dosing, those blasts should mature along the myeloid lineage through the pathway implicated by DHODH-inhibitor experiments [S4]. Second, that maturation program is proposed to be separable from BCL-2–linked oxidative-phosphorylation dependence in ROS-low leukemia stem cells [S1] and from the oxidative, fatty-acid-oxidation-associated state of cytarabine-residual cells [S2]. Third, exogenous uridine is proposed to rescue both nucleotide depletion and the maturation phenotype if, and only if, the effect is on-target at DHODH. That rescue logic is a pathway inference, not a result shown for teriflunomide in this packet.

Alternative explanations. Maturation markers could increase through nonspecific stress or through selective survival of an already more mature subpopulation. Nucleotide depletion could suppress proliferation and viability without engaging the maturation program reported for DHODH inhibition [S4]. An off-target activity of teriflunomide could produce the same surface phenotype. Apparent activity could instead reflect the oxidative-metabolism vulnerability of residual AML [S2] or the BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation vulnerability of quiescent leukemia stem cells [S1], which would place the drug with the venetoclax–azacitidine metabolic comparator [S3]. Pyrimidine content of the culture medium could mask or exaggerate pathway dependence.

Discriminating preclinical test. Compare differentiation-blocked AML samples with matched normal CD34-positive cells across a concentration range that includes verified clinical unbound exposures. Include a uridine-rescue arm, a chemically unrelated DHODH-inhibitor benchmark whose identity is independently confirmed, and venetoclax–azacitidine as the established metabolic comparator [S3]. At fixed times, record morphology and myeloid surface markers, viability and cell-cycle distribution, dihydroorotate and uridine-nucleotide levels, and clonogenic growth. In a cytarabine-residual fraction modeled on the oxidative state in [S2], test whether any loss of viability tracks with maturation or with loss of oxidative-metabolism features. In a ROS-low fraction modeled on [S1], test whether teriflunomide matures bulk blasts while leaving that fraction intact. Normal progenitors provide the selectivity comparison. Model results of this type would not establish clinical efficacy [S2].

Falsifying observation. The drug–mechanism–context claim is disconfirmed if verified multiple-sclerosis–relevant unbound exposure fails to increase myeloid maturation relative to vehicle in differentiation-blocked AML blasts, or if maturation occurs despite uridine rescue and without a change in de novo pyrimidine intermediates. Equivalent loss of normal CD34-positive progenitor function at that exposure also disconfirms a usable selective window. A dominant effect consisting of depletion of ROS-low or cytarabine-residual oxidative cells without a differentiation signature would assign the result to the metabolic contexts in [S1] and [S2] rather than to the DHODH differentiation mechanism in [S4]. Failure of an unrelated DHODH inhibitor to phenocopy teriflunomide under the same conditions would favor an off-target account.

Limitations. Pathway membership alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy. [S4] does not establish that every approved agent affecting DHODH reproduces differentiation or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity, and [S1] does not establish an acceptable window for an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor. Cited model and patient-associated findings do not transfer directly to every AML genotype, to randomized comparative efficacy, or to combination dosing [S1][S2][S3]. Unverified protein binding, tissue exposure, and physiologic uridine could close any window. Loss of leukemic clonogenicity after marker-defined maturation still requires functional confirmation [S4].

Arms: vehicle; teriflunomide at 0.5x, 1x, and 2x label unbound steady state; teriflunomide plus uridine; an electron-transport inhibitor that lowers oxygen consumption; a fatty-acid-oxidation inhibitor; each inhibitor alone and with teriflunomide; venetoclax plus azacitidine as the [S3] comparator; single-agent venetoclax only as an [S1] BCL-2 and oxidative-phosphorylation control; brequinar plus genetic DHODH loss as the on-target benchmark. Gates: dihydroorotate at least 2-fold up and UTP and CTP each at least 50 percent down, reversed by uridine; at least a 15 percentage-point rise in cells positive for two or more of CD11b, CD14, and CD15, with morphologic maturation; at least 50 percent fewer residual leukemic colonies or less engraftment, with normal CD34-positive colonies at least 70 percent of vehicle. Split samples by ROS level.

Falsifying observation. Either missed primary gate at matched unbound exposure falsifies the full claim: differentiation below the 15-point gate, or leukemic residual colonies or engraftment reduced by less than 50 percent. Selectivity fails if normal CD34-positive clonogenicity falls at least as much as the leukemic fraction. No dihydroorotate rise, or no UTP or CTP fall, means DHODH was not engaged. Uridine that fails to restore nucleotides and block the phenotype places the effect outside DHODH. Rescue confined to the cytarabine-pretreated fraction is scored as prior nucleoside stress. Uridine-rescuable differentiation in respiration-low cells, or unchanged dihydroorotate and UTP and CTP after electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation block, falsifies bridge two. Acute loss of oxygen consumption without the differentiation gate, in the pattern of BCL-2 suppression in [S1], falsifies a differentiation mechanism.

Limitations. [S2] and [S4] cover only their summarized residual and differentiation findings. [S1] and [S3] are comparators, so this stays distinct from an established AML regimen. Approval, the unbound 14 mg value, potency, brequinar, and off-target binding remain unverified prior knowledge. The cytarabine schedule is a protocol choice. Nucleoside-rich medium, short follow-up, and unverified hepatic and teratogenic class risks still limit translation.

answer.answer:
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide and an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual human AML at unbound exposures matching the labeled multiple-sclerosis regimen, while normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity than the leukemic residual cells.

Biological context. Specimens split into cytarabine-naive and cytarabine-treated aliquots. Cytarabine dose and schedule follow Farge [S2] after re-reading; the packet states none. The former ≥70% kill gate is retired. Residual cells show mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features across the viability range. Primary analysis uses specimens that remain mostly viable (viable fraction ≥50% of vehicle). Prespecified strata (unverified prior knowledge) are CD34+CD38− versus mature phenotype and NPM1, FLT3-ITD, IDH1/2, and TP53. Differentiation, serial colonies, and engraftment are primary, apart from bulk kill and ROS-low clearance. Normal CD34-positive progenitors test selectivity. Venetoclax plus azacitidine is only the [S3] comparator.

Supported premises. [S2] found cytarabine-resistant human AML inconsistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells, with mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and with response changes when that state was altered. [S4] found DHODH inhibition promoting myeloid differentiation and affecting disease endpoints in tested models. [S1] links BCL-2 inhibition to lower oxidative phosphorylation in ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells. [S3] links venetoclax plus azacitidine to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects in leukemia stem cells.

Unverified prior knowledge. Leflunomide is approved for rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide, its active metabolite, is approved for multiple sclerosis, inhibits DHODH, and is highly protein-bound. Provisional unbound 1× is total mean Css for 14 mg once daily times the free fraction. Recalled values, outside [S1]–[S4] and replaced before dosing by the current label and by free drug in albumin-matched medium, are total Css near 50 μg/mL (185 μM; MW 270.2), binding >99%, free fraction near 0.5%, unbound 1× near 0.9 μM, human DHODH IC50 near 1 μM, and cellular IC50 near 1–5 μM. Unbound 1× more than tenfold below the cellular IC50 makes exposure implausible. DHODH donates electrons to coenzyme Q. Brequinar is an orthogonal inhibitor.

Speculative bridges. Bridge one: at locked unbound 1×, teriflunomide inhibits DHODH, raises dihydroorotate, lowers UTP and CTP, and drives uridine-rescuable differentiation in residual AML. Bridge two: antimycin A depletes oxidized coenzyme Q by slowing ubiquinol reoxidation, stalls DHODH, raises dihydroorotate, and deepens uridine-rescuable nucleotide loss in viable cells; respiratory death stays uridine-refractory [S1][S2]. Idebenone reverses CD11b only if UTP returns. Etomoxir is an [S2] CPT1 survival comparator: clonogenic loss without uridine rescue or differentiation. Bridge three: these effects sit outside the [S1] ROS-low state and the [S3] pattern. Bridge four: normal CD34-positive progenitors retain colonies by salvage, while residual AML links differentiation block to de novo synthesis.

Alternative explanations. Off-target kinase or aryl-hydrocarbon-receptor binding (unverified prior knowledge) may mimic differentiation. Pyrimidine depletion may kill cycling blasts and spare oxidative residual cells. Uridine help only after cytarabine may reflect prior analog stress. Restriction to one genotype or maturation stratum would confine the claim.

Discriminating preclinical test. Drug contact is 96 h, replaced by the [S4] time course if different. Arms are 0.3×, 1×, and 3× locked unbound teriflunomide, with free drug measured. Named tools, doses unverified until titration: antimycin A 0.5 μM, adjusted to a ≥50% fall in basal oxygen consumption; etomoxir 10 μM; idebenone 5 μM with and without teriflunomide. Also vehicle, teriflunomide, teriflunomide plus uridine, venetoclax plus azacitidine [S3], venetoclax alone [S1], and brequinar or DHODH loss. Minimum eight mostly viable, signature-positive specimens. Readouts are CD11b with CD14 or CD15, dihydroorotate, UTP/CTP, oxygen consumption, ROS, three serial platings, and NSG marrow human CD45 at 8–12 weeks after equal viable inocula, plus serial transplant. Colonies and engraftment are joint, paired endpoints. Gates move to the smallest positive DHODH-inhibitor CD11b and nucleotide effects stated in [S4]. Until extracted, 1× success is a ≥20-point CD11b rise co-expressed with CD14 or CD15, uridine reversal of half or more of that rise, ≥2-fold dihydroorotate, ≥40% lower UTP or CTP, ≥50% fewer serial colonies, ≥50% lower engraftment, and <25% loss of normal CD34-positive colonies.

Falsifying observation. Missing the CD11b gate, either leukemic endpoint (loss below 50%), or the normal-colony limit (loss reaching 25%) falsifies the full claim at unbound 1×. No dihydroorotate rise, or nucleotide loss without uridine rescue of CD11b, places the effect outside DHODH. Antimycin without dihydroorotate accumulation fails bridge two. Idebenone that splits UTP recovery from loss of CD11b breaks coupling. Uridine rescue of etomoxir loss falsifies the survival-comparator prediction. Respiratory shutdown without differentiation reproduces [S1]. A hit confined to one stratum, or only to cytarabine-pretreated cells, indicates subset biology or prior nucleotide stress.

Limitations. [S2] and [S4] cover the summarized studies. [S1] and [S3] remain comparators. Approval, exposure, IC50, tool doses, NSG host, off-target binding, and hepatic or teratogenic risk stay unverified prior knowledge. Medium nucleosides can misstate salvage. Short follow-up can miss relapse. Measured free drug defines 1× when medium binding differs from plasma.

ranking.item: Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide and an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual human AML at unbound exposures matching the labeled multiple-sclerosis regimen, while normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity than the leukemic residual cells.

answer.answer:
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of the rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide, at unbound steady-state exposure from its approved multiple-sclerosis regimen, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation and a selective loss of engraftment in cytarabine-residual human AML, while matched normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity.

Biological context. Primary human AML is tested as a cytarabine-residual fraction plus a paired cytarabine-naive aliquot. Primary endpoints are myeloid differentiation and reduced leukemic engraftment or clonogenicity. Bulk killing, oxygen-consumption loss, and clearance of ROS-low leukemia stem cells are separate readouts.

Supported premises. [S2] found cytarabine-resistant human AML cells with inconsistent immature quiescent leukemia-stem-cell enrichment, mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related oxidative metabolism, and response changes when that state was altered. [S4] found that DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in the experimental AML systems tested. [S1] found frequent low reactive oxygen species and elevated BCL-2 in functionally defined leukemia stem cells, with oxidative-phosphorylation loss after BCL-2 inhibition. [S3] linked venetoclax plus azacitidine to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects in leukemia stem cells and is the established combination comparator only.

Unverified prior knowledge requiring a check before dosing: leflunomide is approved for rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide, its active metabolite, is approved for multiple sclerosis and inhibits DHODH; DHODH passes electrons to ubiquinone, whose respiratory reoxidation can support turnover; unbound steady-state levels exist for the approved teriflunomide multiple-sclerosis schedule; brequinar is an orthogonal DHODH inhibitor. None of these facts are in the packet.

Speculative bridges. Bridge one: that unbound exposure engages DHODH, raises dihydroorotate, lowers UTP or CTP, and yields uridine-rescuable differentiation of the [S4] class. Bridge two, respiratory supply alone: residual oxidative metabolism [S2] keeps ubiquinone oxidized so DHODH can turn over. [S2] supports an oxidative-phosphorylation and fatty-acid-oxidation survival dependency, and ubiquinone regeneration is unverified prior knowledge outside [S2]. Bridge three, selective dependence as its own prediction: residual AML draws a larger share of pyrimidines from DHODH-dependent de novo synthesis, and less from salvage, than matched normal CD34-positive progenitors, so leukemic clonogenicity falls further. Bridge four: differentiation and engraftment loss occur outside the ROS-low, BCL-2-high state in [S1] and apart from the [S3] pattern.

Alternative explanations. Unverified off-target kinase or aryl-hydrocarbon-receptor effects could drive the phenotype. Pyrimidine depletion could kill cycling bulk blasts and spare residual oxidative cells and ROS-low stem cells. Uridine rescue after cytarabine, a pyrimidine nucleoside analog, could reflect prior nucleotide stress. Respiratory shutdown without differentiation would copy the vulnerability in [S1] and [S2].

Discriminating preclinical test. Preset residual gate, to be checked against [S2] methods: cytarabine 1 µM for 48 hours, 24-hour washout, dye-excluding cells ≥70 percent of the recovered suspension, residual cell number ≤40 percent of matched vehicle. Exposure is unbound teriflunomide at the verified multiple-sclerosis steady state. Arms: vehicle; teriflunomide; teriflunomide plus uridine; teriflunomide plus electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition; venetoclax plus azacitidine as the [S3] comparator; single-agent venetoclax as the [S1] BCL-2/oxidative-phosphorylation control; brequinar or genetic DHODH loss as the orthogonal benchmark. Respiration-low means oxygen consumption below 50 percent of vehicle after that inhibitor. Readouts: morphology; CD11b with CD14 or CD15; dihydroorotate and UTP/CTP; residual engraftment or colonies; oxygen consumption; normal CD34-positive colonies; ROS split; genotype as a covariate. The naive aliquot and normal CD34-positive cells get the same metabolite and uridine arms. Positive cutoffs: ≥2-fold CD11b and CD14 or CD15 rise; ≥50 percent fall in residual leukemic colonies or CD45-positive engraftment; uridine reversal of ≥50 percent of the differentiation rise; ≥2-fold dihydroorotate rise with ≥30 percent UTP or CTP fall; normal CD34-positive colonies ≥70 percent of vehicle.

Falsifying observations. Either missed primary cutoff falsifies the full claim: differentiation rise below 2-fold, residual leukemic engraftment or clonogenicity falling by under 50 percent, or normal CD34-positive colonies below 70 percent of vehicle. Absent uridine rescue or absent dihydroorotate and UTP/CTP shifts places the effect outside DHODH. Uridine-rescuable differentiation that still reaches 2-fold in respiration-low cells after electron-transport or fatty-acid-oxidation inhibition falsifies bridge two. A selectivity gap without a larger dihydroorotate rise or UTP/CTP fall in residual AML than in normal CD34-positive cells falsifies bridge three. An acute oxygen-consumption fall with differentiation below 2-fold matches [S1] and falsifies a differentiation mechanism. Uridine rescue only in the cytarabine-pretreated aliquot, with dihydroorotate rise in the naive aliquot, counts as prior nucleotide stress.

Limitations. [S2] and [S4] apply only inside the summarized studies. [S1] and [S3] are comparators. Approval, indications, unbound levels, potency, brequinar activity, and off-target binding are unverified prior knowledge. The cytarabine gate is a preset definition. Culture nucleosides can misstate salvage. Short assays can miss an unsampled stem-cell relapse. Hepatic and teratogenic class risks remain unverified prior knowledge and would still limit translation.

answer.answer:
Hypothesis title: Teriflunomide, the active metabolite of rheumatoid-arthritis drug leflunomide and an approved multiple-sclerosis drug, induces uridine-rescuable myeloid differentiation of cytarabine-residual human AML at unbound exposures matching the labeled multiple-sclerosis regimen, while normal CD34-positive progenitors retain greater clonogenicity than the leukemic residual cells.

Biological context. Stratify primary AML by NPM1, FLT3-ITD, IDH1/2, TP53, and primitive versus monocytic state. Copy cytarabine concentration, duration, and washout from the Farge methods before dosing (unverified until checked) [S2]. Define residual cells by a mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation signature at any viability loss. The primary contrast is the mostly viable subset (viability ≥70% of matched vehicle) that carries this signature. Bulk killing, oxidative-phosphorylation loss, and ROS-low clearance are separate scores. Normal CD34-positive progenitors test selectivity. Venetoclax plus azacitidine remains the established [S3] comparator.

Supported premises. [S2] found cytarabine-resistant human AML inconsistently enriched for immature quiescent stem cells, with mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation features, and a response change when that state was altered. [S4] found DHODH inhibition drove myeloid differentiation and disease-endpoint changes in the models tested. [S1] describes ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent stem cells whose oxidative phosphorylation fell after BCL-2 inhibition. [S3] links venetoclax–azacitidine to TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects in leukemia stem cells.

Unverified prior knowledge, locked before dosing. Leflunomide is approved for rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide is approved for multiple sclerosis, inhibits DHODH, and is highly protein-bound. DHODH passes electrons to ubiquinone; complex III regenerates oxidized coenzyme Q, so blocking reoxidation stalls DHODH and deepens pyrimidine depletion. Provisional label math, replaced once the current label is checked: 14 mg once daily, mean total steady-state ≈43 μg/mL (≈159 μM; molecular weight 270.2), protein binding >99%, free fraction 0.5%, so unbound 1× = 0.8 μM (0.3× = 0.24 μM; 3× = 2.4 μM), beside a provisional cellular DHODH IC50 ≈1 μM. Checked 1× more than threefold below that IC50 marks the labeled regimen inactive.

Speculative bridges. Bridge one: 0.8 μM free teriflunomide inhibits DHODH in residual AML, raises dihydroorotate, lowers UTP and CTP, and causes uridine-rescuable [S4]-class differentiation. Bridge two: antimycin A phenocopies that pattern by depleting oxidized coenzyme Q, so differentiation stays uridine-rescuable; with teriflunomide, nucleotide depletion is epistatic, and death that persists during uridine rescue is respiratory toxicity. Idebenone reverses the CD11b shift only if UTP and CTP recover. Bridge three: etomoxir is a separate [S2] survival comparator, predicted to lower residual clonogenicity while dihydroorotate and uridine responsiveness stay unchanged. Bridge four: differentiation and engraftment loss sit outside the [S1] ROS-low state and the [S3] pattern. Bridge five: normal CD34-positive progenitors keep colonies via salvage, and residual AML links the differentiation block to de novo synthesis.

Alternative explanations. Off-target kinase or aryl-hydrocarbon-receptor binding (unverified prior knowledge) may shift markers. Pyrimidine loss may kill cycling bulk blasts and spare oxidative residual cells and ROS-low stem cells. Uridine help only after cytarabine may relieve prior nucleotide stress. Equal DHODH dependence in normal progenitors would close the window.

Discriminating preclinical test. Enroll ≥8 signature-positive, mostly viable specimens from ≥2 genotypes, plus 4 normal CD34-positive donors. Expose cells for the [S4] differentiation interval (provisional 96 h) and measure free drug in albumin-matched medium. Arms: vehicle; teriflunomide 0.3–3×; teriflunomide plus uridine ([S4] rescue dose; provisional 100 μM); antimycin A ± teriflunomide ± uridine, at the lowest 10–1000 nM dose that cuts oxygen consumption ≥50% (ceiling 1 μM); idebenone (provisional 10 μM) ± teriflunomide; etomoxir 10 μM only if oxygen consumption falls <50%; brequinar or genetic DHODH loss at the [S4] concentration (provisional 500 nM); venetoclax–azacitidine at [S3] doses; venetoclax alone as the [S1] control. Read morphology, CD11b with CD14 or CD15, dihydroorotate, UTP/CTP, two serial colony replatings, and paired human CD45+ marrow engraftment in NSG mice at 8–12 weeks (host timing unverified). Both leukemic readouts must pass. Until [S4] effect sizes replace them, 1× thresholds are a ≥20 percentage-point CD11b gain, uridine reversal of at least half that gain, a ≥2-fold dihydroorotate rise, and a ≥40% UTP or CTP drop, plus ≥50% losses of leukemic colonies and of engraftment, with <25% loss of normal colonies.

Falsifying observation. Any primary miss at 1× falsifies the full claim, as do failed uridine rescue and nucleotide change without dihydroorotate accumulation. Antimycin A that suppresses respiration without raising dihydroorotate fails the phenocopy. Idebenone that erases CD11b while UTP/CTP stay low falsifies on-target reversal. Etomoxir that causes uridine-rescuable differentiation invalidates the survival arm. Effects limited to one stratum, or only to cytarabine-pretreated cells, falsify a general residual DHODH claim. Respiration loss without differentiation matches [S1].

Limitations. [S2] and [S4] cover only those studies; [S1] and [S3] are comparators, so this stays distinct from an established AML regimen. Approval, the 43 μg/mL and 0.5% figures, the ~1 μM IC50, tool doses, NSG timing, and hepatic or teratogenic risk remain unverified prior knowledge. Medium nucleosides can distort salvage, and short assays can miss later relapse.
